📝Left Without Aluminum📝

Bloomberg is sounding the alarm — the USA risks running out of high-purity aluminum for defense manufacturing. It turns out that the supply chain for this metal, which is critical for producing fighter jets and armored vehicles, may not withstand a major conflict.

🔻How did this happen?

▪️Last summer, the Pentagon, with direct participation from officials and industry representatives, conducted a classified war game that revealed the USA has virtually stopped producing this alloy.

▪️The only major domestic producer, Century Aluminum plant in Kentucky, capable of producing 99.99% purity aluminum, shut down its production line back in 2022. The reason was an energy crisis and a sharp spike in electricity prices amid the Ukrainian conflict. The plant never reopened, and its facilities were ultimately sold for data center construction.

▪️As a result, the government became completely dependent on imports. Today, about 90% of high-purity aluminum supplies to the US come from the UAE, primarily from the state-owned company Emirates Global Aluminium.

▪️However, military operations against Iran and drone strikes on aluminum plants in the Persian Gulf seriously disrupted logistics, while the blockade of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz drove metal prices to a four-year high. The logistics crisis hit at the worst possible moment, when the Pentagon needed to urgently replenish depleted arsenals.

📌 It should be noted that the country formally retains one operating plant capable of producing aluminum of sufficient purity for military aviation and armored vehicles — the Arconic facility in Davenport. However, military demand accounts for only about 3% of total US aluminum production, so military orders alone are insufficient to maintain large-scale specialized production without imports.

🖍The Trump administration, of course, is trying to fix the situation and bring production back home. Last summer, the USA already raised tariffs on imported aluminum to 50%, and recently Trump signed an executive order on incentives: investors can import metal at a reduced rate, but only if they build new plants within the country.

❗️However, tariffs alone proved insufficient to revive the energy-intensive American industry, and now the White House has to urgently introduce direct incentives to somehow strengthen the production base in case of future conflicts.
